title: Field theory guides Monte Carlo in the one-dimensional long-range Ising model
abstract: The statistical long-range Ising (LRI) model in one dimension provides a family of some of the simplest non-exactly solvable critical points. These critical points are described by long-range conformal field theories (CFTs) that are well understood analytically with perturbative expansions and some exact results. Guided by this, we revisit the Monte Carlo (MC) approach to the corresponding lattice model which has many favorable features compared to other systems studied with MC methods. In particular, with very modest computational cost, we are able to estimate scaling dimensions of leading and subleading operators as well as the associated three-point functions, and even certain four-point functions. These results help highlight the fact that 1d LRI CFTs are a phenomenal playground to more generally test non-perturbative methods and ideas for strongly coupled CFTs.
summary: This work investigates the one-dimensional long-range Ising model, treating it as a testbed for non-perturbative Conformal Field Theory methods. By employing sophisticated Monte Carlo simulations, the authors estimate critical exponents and correlation functions. The results demonstrate the utility of these numerical tools for analyzing complex, strongly coupled quantum many-body systems.
main_problem: The paper revisits the Monte Carlo approach to the one-dimensional long-range Ising (LRI) model to estimate scaling dimensions and correlation functions, using it as a testbed for non-perturbative methods in strongly coupled CFTs.
main_result: The LRI model is shown to be an ideal playground for testing non-perturbative CFT methods, yielding specific estimates for scaling dimensions ($\Delta\phi_2, \Delta\phi_4$) and OPE coefficients through numerical simulations.
method: The study combines field theory analysis (CFT, AdS/CFT correspondence) with advanced numerical techniques, primarily Monte Carlo simulations using optimized algorithms like the Fukui-Todo method.
model_or_system: The system is the one-dimensional long-range Ising (LRI) model, described by a Hamiltonian involving interactions decaying with distance $d(i, j)^{1+s}$. The continuum limit is governed by a Gaussian Free Field (GFF) action.
key_observables: Scaling dimensions of operators ($\Delta\phi_2, \Delta\phi_4$), three-point and four-point functions, the critical coupling constant ($J_{0,c}$), and the Binder cumulant ($U_L$).
important_parameters: The long-range decay exponent ($s$), the coupling constant ($J_0$), and the system size ($L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing results from various estimators and assuming that the system can be mapped to a CFT framework, though systematic uncertainties remain a limitation.
figures_summary: Figures show finite-size scaling of the Binder cumulant ($U_L$) and rescaled propagators ($F_L$) to estimate critical couplings ($J_{0,c}$) for various $s$. Other figures compare calculated scaling dimensions and OPE coefficients across different $s$ values.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using CFT and AdS/CFT for the LRI model. It then details the numerical implementation using efficient MC algorithms to calculate observables like scaling dimensions and correlation functions, culminating in comparisons across different coupling regimes ($s$).
why_interesting: The application of advanced numerical techniques (MC) to study critical phenomena in a solvable, yet complex, CFT model provides a valuable benchmark for developing and testing non-perturbative methods applicable to strongly coupled quantum systems.

Figure 2: Further zoom of fig. 1 in the critical region. Red crosses mark intersections of fits at consecutive lattice sizes. Dashed curves are linear fits over 0.1810 ≤J0 ≤0.1813.

Figure 3: Finite-size critical-coupling estimates at s = 0.4 from the Binder threshold (blue circles) and consecutive-size crossings of FL (orange squares). The x-axis coordinate is the larger size in each pair. Solid curves fit J0,c(L) = J0,c + AL−p and dashed lines represent the extrapolated values. One-standard-error uncertainties are represented by bands.
Figure 4: Same as fig. 3, but for s = 0.9, where the fixed-point in non-Gaussian and the Binder cumulant provides a more stable estimate of the critical coupling.
